title: Predict how by-value parameters, ref, out, in and ref returns affect caller storage, and which method a call runs under virtual dispatch, member hiding, extension lookup and overload resolution

options: Because `Tick` is not marked `readonly` and could write to storage that `in` makes readonly, the compiler calls it on a hidden copy of `b`; with `ref`, `Tick` runs directly on `a`.
Because an `in` struct argument is copied into the parameter exactly like an ordinary by-value argument, `Tick` changes the method's own copy; `ref` passes the caller's variable itself.
Because the runtime rolls back any field writes made through an `in` parameter when the method returns, the change to `b` is lost; `ref` keeps writes made during the call.
Because struct method calls always run on a copy of `this`, `Tick` never touches either variable directly; `ref` additionally copies the result back into `a` after the call.

rubric.point: Selects the option explaining that the compiler makes a defensive copy for a non-readonly method called on an `in` parameter, while `ref` runs the method on the caller's variable.

questions.model: The first option. `in` passes a readonly alias to `b`, not a by-value copy. `Tick` is not `readonly`, so it might write to that readonly storage; the compiler therefore runs it on a defensive copy, and the increment lands on the copy. Through `ref`, `Tick` runs on `a` itself, so `a.Reading` becomes 6.

rubric.point: States that the extension method runs (prints "extension").

Explains that the call is bound at compile time using the variable's compile-time type `Base`: lookup finds no instance `Describe` on `Base`, so the applicable extension is selected, and the runtime type `Derived` is not consulted (no virtual dispatch is involved).

questions.model: The extension method runs and prints `extension`. Lookup uses the compile-time type `Base`, which has no instance `Describe`, so the compiler binds the call to the applicable extension for `Base`. The object's runtime type, `Derived`, is not consulted, because this is a compile-time choice and not virtual dispatch.

c1.feedback: The answer is “Because `Tick` is not marked `readonly` and could write to storage that `in` makes readonly, the compiler calls it on a hidden copy of `b`; with `ref`, `Tick` runs directly on `a`.”.
